messages.subject: Latent variable model/FMM efficiency
parts:
Hello everyone,

I've constructed a (partially) latent variable model where the latent variable (Z in {0, 1}) is then used a predictor within a finite mixture of regressions. Mixture membership is naturally also a latent variable. The likelihood is given by p(Z|X) {p(M|X, Z)P(V|X, Z, M)} P(Y|X, Z, M, V), where the mixture of regressions is in braces, Z is the binary latent variable, M is component membership (M in {0, 1}), V is the outcome variable for the mixture of regressions, Y is a response to a survey question used to identify Z, and X are covariates.

In any case, I have a model that appears to work with simulated data. The model is slow on its own, but with the actual data (~12,000 observations), the model is extremely slow, which I'm okay with if it's working. But I wonder if there's a way to vectorize it or optimize it otherwise. I can't see to find any example in the mailing list where optimizations are done for a finite mixture model.

Lastly, because finite mixture models seem to get stuck in lower probability modes of the posterior analogous to getting stuck in local maxima when using EM, I wonder if there's any way to deal with this in a systematic way. My first thought was simply to run many chains and then use only those chains with the (same) highest lp__. Is this reasonable, or how might one deal with this otherwise in practice? I have a version of this same model as I coded from scratch using EM, but I get separation, so I figured I'd move to STAN, which I've wanted to do for some time and now have reason to do so thankfully.

The model is defined as follows, with simulation / model code attached to this message.

I would really appreciate any help with this. I'd also like to extend my thanks to everyone who has put effort into the STAN project as a whole.

data {
   int N;
   int J;
   int y[N];
   int b1[N];
   real c1[N];
   real c2[N];
   real c3[N];
   int o[N];

   int trials;
   int treat[N];
}
transformed data{
  
  // Respondent types (observed Z = 1, observed Z = 0, latent Z = 0 or 1)
  vector[N] type0;
  vector[N] type1;
  vector[N] type01;

  type0 <- rep_vector(0, N);
  type1 <- rep_vector(0, N);
  type01 <- rep_vector(0, N);

  for(i in 1:N){
    if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == 0) type0[i] <- 1;
    if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == (J + 1)) type1[i] <- 1;
    if(y[i] > 0 && y[i] < (J + 1)) type01[i] <- 1;
    if(treat[i] == 0) type01[i] <- 1;
  }

}

   real control_beta[3 + 0]; // Control items (intercept, Z, U, ...)
   real sens_beta[1 + 0];    // Sensitive item (intercept, ...)

   real outA_beta[2 + 0];    // Outcome regression A (intercept, Z, ...)
   real outB_beta[1 + 0];    // Outcome regression B (intercept, ...)

  control_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  sens_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  concom_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  outA_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  outB_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

  for(i in 1:N){
      
      # IF Z = 0
      if(type0[i] == 1){
        increment_log_prob(
                log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(0, sens_beta[1]) +
                            bernoulli_logit_log(1,
                                                concom_beta[1] +
                                                concom_beta[2] * 0) +
                            binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials,
                                               outA_beta[1] +
                                               outA_beta[2] * 0) +
                            binomial_logit_log(y[i], J,
                                               control_beta[1] +

to save computations and reuse them.

The "+ 0" is just a placeholder because this is the most basic model specification. I've written this for bookkeeping purposes. The full model includes many covariates in each regression and the finite mixture is of beta-binoimal regressions.  This is also the reason for my multiplying some of the parameters by 0 and 1 in the likelihood. If there's anything on the sampling side that could be done, that would be lovely, but I can try to put more informative priors if that's the only way around this at the moment.

Thanks again,
Greg

The chains that have the highest mean lp___ (e.g. that in purple) are the ones that cover the population values for each parameter as I've defined them. On Sunday, June 7, 2015 at 3:39:02 PM UTC-4, Gregory wrote:
Hello everyone,

I've constructed a (partially) latent variable model where the latent variable (Z in {0, 1}) is then used a predictor within a finite mixture of regressions. Mixture membership is naturally also a latent variable. The likelihood is given by p(Z|X) {p(M|X, Z)P(V|X, Z, M)} P(Y|X, Z, M, V), where the mixture of regressions is in braces, Z is the binary latent variable, M is component membership (M in {0, 1}), V is the outcome variable for the mixture of regressions, Y is a response to a survey question used to identify Z, and X are covariates.

In any case, I have a model that appears to work with simulated data. The model is slow on its own, but with the actual data (~12,000 observations), the model is extremely slow, which I'm okay with if it's working. But I wonder if there's a way to vectorize it or optimize it otherwise. I can't see to find any example in the mailing list where optimizations are done for a finite mixture model.

Lastly, because finite mixture models seem to get stuck in lower probability modes of the posterior analogous to getting stuck in local maxima when using EM, I wonder if there's any way to deal with this in a systematic way. My first thought was simply to run many chains and then use only those chains with the (same) highest lp__. Is this reasonable, or how might one deal with this otherwise in practice? I have a version of this same model as I coded from scratch using EM, but I get separation, so I figured I'd move to STAN, which I've wanted to do for some time and now have reason to do so thankfully.

}

  type0 <- rep_vector(0, N);
  type1 <- rep_vector(0, N);
  type01 <- rep_vector(0, N);

  for(i in 1:N){
    if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == 0) type0[i] <- 1;
    if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == (J + 1)) type1[i] <- 1;
    if(y[i] > 0 && y[i] < (J + 1)) type01[i] <- 1;
    if(treat[i] == 0) type01[i] <- 1;
  }

                            bernoulli_logit_log(1,

                            binomial_logit_log(y[i] - treat[i], J,
                                               control_beta[1] +
                                               control_beta[2] * 1 +
                                               control_beta[3] * 1),

                            bernoulli_logit_log(1, sens_beta[1]) +
                            bernoulli_logit_log(0,

                            binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials, outB_beta[1]) +
                            binomial_logit_log(y[i] - treat[i], J,
                                               control_beta[1] +

        );

Although you may need to justify stronger priors, the alternative is justifying
you're doing the right thing inferentially for a multimodal prior, which is

I'm afraid we don't have any good techniques (for the moment at least in Stan) for
dealing with multimodality that doesn't mix within a single chain.
